summary: The 2026 FIFA World Cup wrapped in downtown Atlanta this week after a wild England versus Argentina semifinal at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, closing out four years of buildup and reshaping a chunk of the city along the way. Decatur's free WatchFest packed the Square for the same match, and the city says one World Cup upgrade is sticking around: 60% fewer potholes downtown. In the West End, Soul Vegetarian, Atlanta's oldest Black-owned vegan restaurant, closed after 47 years. Atlanta marks 30 years since the 1996 Olympics with a documentary screening, the Decatur Book Festival announced its fall author lineup, FNF Hot Burger is heading to Phipps Plaza, and Decatur native Jordan Walker took home the MLB Home Run Derby title.

topStory.headline: Atlanta's World Cup Goes Out With a Bang After England-Argentina Semifinal
topStory.summary: Four years of buildup ended Wednesday in downtown Atlanta, where an England versus Argentina semifinal at Mercedes-Benz Stadium capped the biggest sporting spectacle the city has hosted since the 1996 Olympics.
topStory.body: It is over, and what a run it was. The 2026 FIFA World Cup closed out its Atlanta chapter Wednesday with an England versus Argentina semifinal at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, and Downtown turned into one long street party. Four years of hype and great expectations culminated in a single electric day, according to Urbanize Atlanta, which described a section of the city physically and maybe fundamentally changed by its largest sporting event since the 1996 Games. Whether you were pulling for England or Argentina, the consensus around the plaza was the same: what a party. Atlanta landed a marquee slate of matches as one of the tournament's American host cities, and the crowds downtown made the most of every one of them. Watch parties spilled out of bars and onto street corners, into public parks and squares, until the World Cup became, for a few weeks, just part of local life. Now the tents come down and the city takes stock. A World Cup does not leave a place the way it found it, and Atlanta spent years preparing its roads, its transit, and its downtown core for the world's arrival. The visitors are heading home. A lot of what got built and fixed for them is staying put.
topStory.imageAlt: Fans fill downtown Atlanta near Mercedes-Benz Stadium for the World Cup semifinal

stories.headline: Decatur WatchFest Packs the Square for Argentina's Upset of England
stories.summary: Soccer fans filled Decatur Square on a humid Wednesday afternoon to watch Argentina stun England in the World Cup semifinal on the free public screens.
stories.body: You did not need a Mercedes-Benz Stadium ticket to feel the semifinal. You needed a spot on Decatur Square. Fans flocked to the Square on a warm, humid Wednesday afternoon, July 15, to watch England take on Argentina in the FIFA World Cup semifinal, according to Decaturish. By the final whistle, Argentina had knocked out England and sent the crowd home buzzing. Decatur WatchFest has been one of metro Atlanta's biggest gathering spots all tournament, drawing six figures of visitors to free viewing on giant public screens. For a small city that leans hard into its downtown, a packed Square for a World Cup semifinal is exactly the kind of thing Decatur likes to be known for.
stories.imageAlt: Crowds watch the World Cup semifinal on big screens at Decatur Square

stories.headline: Atlanta Marks 30 Years Since the 1996 Olympics With a Documentary Screening
stories.summary: A screening of the local film 'The Games in Black & White' at the Tara Theatre celebrates three decades since the torch touched down at Atlanta City Hall.
stories.body: On July 18, 1996, the Olympic torch touched down at Atlanta City Hall. Thirty years later, a group of Olympic aficionados is marking the anniversary with a screening at the Tara Theatre, according to SaportaReport. The film is the award-winning local documentary "The Games in Black & White," which tells the story of the partnership between Andrew Young and Billy Payne that won Atlanta the 1996 Games, from the bid through the Games themselves to the legacy they left behind. It premiered at the 2025 Atlanta Film Festival and later aired on Georgia Public Broadcasting. The timing lands well. Atlanta just wrapped a World Cup that reshaped its Downtown the way the Olympics did a generation ago, so a look back at what the last mega-event actually left behind feels earned.
stories.imageAlt: Promotional image for the documentary The Games in Black and White about the 1996 Atlanta Olympics

stories.headline: Decatur Book Festival Reveals Its First Wave of 2026 Authors
stories.summary: The Oct. 2-3 festival announced 16 authors, including Pulitzer winner Brian Goldstone, novelist Tayari Jones, and U.S. Poet Laureate Arthur Sze.
stories.body: The Decatur Book Festival has revealed the first 16 authors on the bill for its 2026 event, set for Oct. 2 and 3 in Decatur. The early lineup is heavy hitting. Pulitzer Prize winner Brian Goldstone gives the keynote on Friday, Oct. 2. Children's authors Katherine Applegate and Gennifer Choldenko headline a Saturday "Kidnote" session, New York Times bestselling author Tomi Adeyemi opens the festival morning for young adult readers, and the roster also includes the 25th U.S. Poet Laureate Arthur Sze and award-winning novelist Tayari Jones. The Decatur Book Festival is one of the largest independent book festivals in the country, and it has long been a fixture of the fall calendar for intown readers. More authors are expected before October.
stories.imageAlt: Decatur Book Festival 2026 author lineup announcement

stories.headline: Soul Vegetarian, Atlanta's Oldest Black-Owned Vegan Restaurant, Closes After 47 Years
stories.summary: The West End institution served its last meals on July 12, ending a run that fed generations of intown diners across nearly five decades.
stories.body: After 47 years, Atlanta's oldest Black-owned vegan restaurant has closed its doors. Soul Vegetarian in the West End served its final meals on July 12, according to The Atlanta Voice. In its last days, the restaurant filled with regulars saying goodbye. One woman who had been coming since she was a child shared a meal with her teenage son, two generations connected by the same West End kitchen. That kind of loyalty is what made Soul Vegetarian more than a restaurant. Opened in 1979, it was a pioneer of plant-based cooking in Atlanta long before vegan food went mainstream, and it anchored a stretch of the West End for decades. Its closing marks the end of a real chapter for the neighborhood and for the city's Black food history.
stories.imageAlt: Chef Pahroosha Israel outside Soul Vegetarian in the West End

stories.headline: FNF Hot Burger Is Bringing Its Spicy Smash Patties to Phipps Plaza
stories.summary: The homegrown burger brand, born in Decatur and now in East Atlanta, adds a third spot in the Phipps Plaza food hall this summer.
stories.body: FNF Hot Burger is expanding again, this time to Buckhead. The local brand plans to open on the first floor of the Phipps Plaza food hall this summer, according to What Now Atlanta. The spot is awaiting final permitting, which will set the exact opening date, with a grand opening planned for later this summer. Founder Vic Tran launched FNF in Decatur in early 2025 while chasing the perfect spicy smash burger, then added a location at the Halidom Eatery food hall in East Atlanta. Phipps makes three, and it keeps a fast-growing intown brand on its run through the food halls that have become launchpads for Atlanta's independent restaurants.
stories.imageAlt: FNF Hot Burger spicy smash burger heading to Phipps Plaza

stories.headline: Downtown Atlanta Has 60% Fewer Potholes After the World Cup Road Push
stories.summary: The city says a pre-tournament infrastructure effort left downtown pavement rated 'good' instead of 'fair,' and the improvement is here to stay.
stories.body: The World Cup may be over, but city officials say one upgrade is sticking around: smoother roads. The Atlanta Department of Transportation says Downtown now has 60% fewer potholes than it did in 2024, according to WSB-TV. The repairs came out of a major push that began well ahead of the tournament, when crews used vehicle-mounted road scanners to map pavement damage across the city and target the worst corridors first. Downtown's pavement rating climbed from "fair" to "good" on a 100-point scale as a result. City officials liked the results enough to keep the road-scanning program running past the World Cup. So if you spot a car with an odd device mounted on its roof, it is out there logging the next round of repairs.
stories.imageAlt: Road crews repair downtown Atlanta pavement ahead of the World Cup

stories.headline: Home Run Derby Champ Jordan Walker Got His Start in Decatur
stories.summary: The slugger who took home this year's MLB Home Run Derby title traces his baseball roots back to Decatur.
stories.body: This year's MLB Home Run Derby champion is a Decatur product. Jordan Walker, who outlasted the field to win the derby, began his baseball journey in Decatur, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. Walker came up through metro Atlanta baseball before turning into one of the game's most powerful young hitters, and a national showcase like the derby is a good moment for local fans to claim him. The long ball has always played well in this town, and watching a hometown kid win the sport's biggest power contest is the kind of story Decatur will happily take.
stories.imageAlt: Jordan Walker, Decatur native and MLB Home Run Derby champion
